newsitem.title: UK: Eurobonds see Britain tap dollars, Denmark in marks.
newsitem.headline: Eurobonds see Britain tap dollars, Denmark in marks.

text.p: The highlight of the Euromarket on Thursday was the launch of Britain's second Eurobond in two months, an equally successful $2.0 billion five-year callable FRN. The issue came after weeks of vague speculation Britain was planning something big.

"As far as the market is concerned, this is a surprise. That's the way the Bank (of England) prefers to do it," said one new issues manager at a British bank close to the deal. "It was sprung on the market with very little warning," said another.
On July 15, Britain issued a $2.0 billion five-year fixed-rate bond.
It was priced at a five basis points yield spread over U.S. Treasuries via Goldman Sachs International and SBC Warburg and was judged a big success.

Added to the list of sovereign borrowers, Denmark raised 500 million marks over five years via joint lead managers SBC Warburg and Nomura. The bond pays a five percent coupon and yields 17 basis points over Bunds.
The country last tapped marks in February with a 300 million mark December 1999 bond flat to Bunds.
Syndicate manager at SBC Warburg said the bond was targeted at Swiss retail and institutional investors.
The Bank of England said the issue was for routine debt management purposes and the proceeds would complete the refinancing of the $4.0 billion FRN.
Today's issue, which will be callable at par on coupon dates from October 1999, was reoffered at the 99.745 issue price for a margin of 19 basis points below three-month LIBOR.
The new paper will pay 12.5 basis points below three-month LIBID, the same as the maturing paper. BZW was bookrunner and joint lead manager with HSBC Markets and NatWest Markets.
Traders said the pricing - three-month Libor minus 19 b.p. - reflected the quality of the borrower.
BZW said the pricing was between six and seven b.p. through where other quality sovereign FRNs were trading last night.

Distribution was said to be very widespread, and final geographical breakdown was around 30 percent in Asia (including Japan), 60 percent in Middle East and Europe (including the UK) and 10 percent elsewhere -- offshore U.S. accounts, African central banks and Latin America. Added to this, many bank's funds would have to have the paper in their portfolios.
They said Britain opted for an FRN because of a shortage of high-quality paper in the market. Britain's previous deal in July was its first Eurobond since 1992.
He said the lack of secondary market sovereign mark paper had boosted demand and enabled a tighter launch spread.
Following the positive French 1997 budget and a successful roadshow in France, Electrolux launched a 1.0 billion French franc eight-year bond to yield 52 b.p. over French government paper.

A syndicate official at Banque Nationale de Paris said the bond had sold to French retail and institutional investors who were attracted by the rarity of the borrower (the world's largest provider of white goods) in the market.
Electrolux is rated BAA2 by Moody's Investors Service.
Electrolux last raised French francs in 1988, a 500 million franc, June 1995, 9.125 percent bond.
Paribas Capital Markets led-managed a $100 million five-year Morocco-linked bond for Morocco Investments Ltd.
The bond is callable at par after three years, yields 340 b.p. over Treasuries and is backed by Morocco tranche A loans.
The EBRD set a 1.0 billion Czech crown two-year bond via Wood-Commerz. The bond pays an 11.0 percent coupon.
Recently a Deutsche Bank unit set a 1.0 billion Czech crown one-year bond which paid an 11.50 percent bond.
-- Hayley Pienaar, London Newsroom +44 171 542 7718
